question: What main fuel do brain cells (neurons) need constantly to keep working hard?
explanation: Neurons are very busy cells! They rely heavily on a continuous supply of glucose and oxygen to keep their energy up and function properly. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T19#GNS222_U3_T19_h1)

question: Why is brain damage often permanent, unlike injuries in other parts of the body?

options.A: Neurons have a very limited capacity to regenerate once destroyed.
options.B: Neurons reproduce too rapidly for normal cellular repair mechanisms.
options.C: Surrounding glial cells actively prevent any blood flow to the area.
options.D: Neurons store excessive amounts of toxic waste products.

explanation: Unlike skin or muscle tissue, mature brain cells don't easily divide or replace themselves. Once lost, it's very hard for them to grow back. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T19#GNS222_U3_T19_h1)

question: Which chemical messenger causes major damage to brain cells when it is released in excess during an injury?
explanation: Too much glutamate overexcites the brain cells, opening the gates for a dangerous rush of calcium ions that can damage the cell. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T19#GNS222_U3_T19_h2)

question: What is the big worry with secondary brain injuries after a sudden head trauma or stroke?

options.A: Cellular damage continues to unfold over hours and days after the initial insult.
options.B: All injured neurons instantly recover full electrical function within minutes.
options.C: Blood pressure drops to zero throughout the entire systemic circulation.
options.D: The immune system completely stops responding to any external pathogens.

explanation: Even after the primary event stops, things like swelling and chemical stress keep destroying tissue over the next few hours or days. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T19#GNS222_U3_T19_h2)

question: What are the three main things that fill up the space inside your hard skull?

options.A: Neurons, glial cells, and extracellular matrix
options.B: Brain tissue, blood, and cerebrospinal fluid
options.C: Skull bone, scalp muscle, and interstitial fluid
options.D: Venous plasma, arterial blood, and lymph fluid

explanation: Think of the skull as a closed box. Inside, you only have brain tissue, blood, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sharing that fixed space. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T19#GNS222_U3_T19_h3)

question: If a brain tumor starts growing inside the skull, what has to happen first to keep pressure from rising too high?

options.A: Brain neurons must shrink in size to increase internal air pockets.
options.B: The bones of the skull must stretch outward to create more space.
options.C: Cerebrospinal fluid or blood volume must decrease to compensate.
options.D: Systemic heart rate must drop to zero to halt blood entering the head.

explanation: Since an adult skull cannot stretch, the body makes room for the new mass by pushing out some CSF or blood. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T19#GNS222_U3_T19_h3)

question: What is the main cause of an ischemic stroke?

options.A: Sudden systemic drop in normal body temperature
options.B: Uncontrolled electrical discharge across the motor cortex
options.C: Rupture of a weakened blood vessel inside the brain tissue
options.D: Occlusion of a cerebral artery by a thrombus or embolus

explanation: An ischemic stroke happens when a blood clot blocks a brain vessel, cutting off the oxygen and nutrients that part of the brain needs. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T19#GNS222_U3_T19_h4)

question: Why do brain cells start swelling up (edema) when they run out of energy during a stroke?

options.A: The skull instantly expands to pull excess fluid out of the bloodstream.
options.B: The sodium-potassium pump stops working, allowing water and sodium to rush inside.
options.C: Damaged neurons start producing excess amounts of fatty storage oils.
options.D: Red blood cells leak out of intact capillaries and flood the ventricles.

explanation: Without energy (ATP), tiny cellular pumps fail. Sodium and water rush into the cell, making it swell up like a balloon. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T19#GNS222_U3_T19_h4)

question: Which neurotransmitter works to calm down electrical activity in the brain and balance things out?
explanation: GABA is the brain's main 'braking' system. It helps calm down nerve activity so things don't get too excited. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T19#GNS222_U3_T19_h5)

question: What happens in the brain during a seizure that puts cells at risk of injury?

options.A: Brain tissue instantly freezes due to a sudden halt in all chemical reactions.
options.B: Neurons fire excessively and synchronously, causing a massive spike in metabolic and oxygen demand.
options.C: Inhibitory neurotransmitters multiply rapidly and shut down all electrical signals.
options.D: Blood flow completely stops to every part of the brain simultaneously.

explanation: During a seizure, brain cells fire wildly all at once. They burn through energy and oxygen way faster than the body can supply it. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T19#GNS222_U3_T19_h5)

question: What is the common underlying problem in chronic brain diseases like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's?

options.A: Acute bacterial infection inside the ventricular system
options.B: Complete destruction of the skull bone structure
options.C: Abnormal folding and accumulation of specific proteins
options.D: Sudden rupture of major cerebral aneurysms

explanation: In these conditions, certain proteins misfold and clump together into sticky clusters that slowly harm brain cells over time. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T19#GNS222_U3_T19_h6)

question: Which specific brain cells are mainly destroyed in Parkinson's disease?

options.A: Cholinergic neurons in the peripheral nerves
options.B: Upper motor neurons in the cerebral cortex
options.C: Sensory neurons in the dorsal root ganglia
options.D: Dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra

explanation: Parkinson's specifically targets the cells that make dopamine in a brain area called the substantia nigra, affecting movement. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T19#GNS222_U3_T19_h6)

question: What is the main job of the myelin sheath wrapped around a nerve fiber?

options.A: To insulate the axon and ensure rapid conduction of electrical impulses
options.B: To produce neurotransmitters for chemical synapse transmission
options.C: To anchor the neuron firmly to surrounding skull bones
options.D: To supply continuous glucose and oxygen directly to the cell nucleus

explanation: Think of myelin like the plastic insulation around an electrical wire. It helps messages zip down the nerve fiber super fast! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T19#GNS222_U3_T19_h7)

question: What goes wrong in the body to cause the symptoms of multiple sclerosis (MS)?

options.A: Accumulation of beta-amyloid plaques in the temporal lobes
options.B: Excessive release of glutamate causing immediate excitotoxicity
options.C: Thrombus formation blocking blood flow in the middle cerebral artery
options.D: Autoimmune destruction of central nervous system myelin

explanation: In MS, the body's immune system mistakenly attacks and strips away the protective myelin coating on nerve fibers, slowing down signals. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T19#GNS222_U3_T19_h7)

question: What is usually the very first warning sign that a patient's intracranial pressure (ICP) is rising?

options.A: A sudden drop in core body temperature
options.B: A complete loss of all deep tendon reflexes
options.C: A subtle change in the level of consciousness
options.D: A severe decrease in peripheral blood pressure

explanation: Before vitals change dramatically, patients usually get a bit confused, restless, or sleepier than usual when pressure starts building. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T19#GNS222_U3_T19_h8)

question: A patient with a head injury has one pupil that is large and doesn't react well to light. What does this usually suggest?

options.A: An allergic reaction to systemic intravenous antibiotic therapy
options.B: A minor scalp laceration healing normally without complication
options.C: Compression of cranial nerve III due to brain herniation
options.D: Permanent regeneration of damaged peripheral nerve pathways

explanation: When pressure pushes brain tissue downward, it can squeeze cranial nerve III, which controls the pupil. This causes that classic 'fixed and dilated' pupil. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T19#GNS222_U3_T19_h8)
